title: A metric ellipse field: how does local distance scale vary?
summary: At each grid point a small ellipse shows the set of unit-length vectors under the local metric. A small ellipse means distance is costly in those directions; a large ellipse means it is cheap. Direction and anisotropy are read from the ellipse axes.

media.alt: A grid of teal ellipses, large and nearly round at the bottom left, smaller and tilted toward the right and top, with a dashed orange reference circle and the note 'legend: g = I' at the right.
media.caption: Reference render of class F2.7 (design-system gallery). The data are synthetic and exist only to demonstrate the form.

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data. Standard theory only.

read_the_figure.question: How does local distance scale vary?
read_the_figure.axes: x and y in the plane, equal scale. Each ellipse is centred on a grid point (x from 0 to 4, y from 0 to 3). Its shape is the set {v : g(v, v) = 1}, drawn at 0.21 of its true size. The dashed orange circle at the right is the Euclidean reference g = identity, with radius 0.21.
look_at: Where are the ellipses biggest and where smallest? Compare each to the dashed reference circle.
Where are they most elongated (strongly anisotropic) and in which direction?
How do the long axes turn as you move across the grid?
Is distance cheaper along the long axis or along the short axis?
as_drawn: The metric is g = R(phi) diag(l1, l2) R(phi)^T with phi = 0.5y + 0.2x, l1 = 1.4 + 1.6x/4 and l2 = 1 + 2.2y/3. At (0, 0) the eigenvalues are 1 and 1.4; at (4, 3) they are 3.0 and 3.2.
Big ellipse at the bottom-left, small and nearly round at the top-right: distance is about 1.7 times more costly there, nearly the same in all directions.
A reference circle for g = I is drawn at the right, so the reader can read absolute size. The note at top says small axis = long distance cost.
read_the_figure.proves: How the local metric varies over the sampled grid: relative size, anisotropy and orientation. It does not show curvature, geodesics or the metric between grid points.
if_wrong: No reference circle: the ellipse sizes have no absolute meaning.
Ellipses so large that they overlap: shape and orientation become unreadable.
The inverse convention (unit ball of the inverse metric) used silently: big and small swap.

terms.meaning: A symmetric positive matrix at each point that gives lengths: |v| = sqrt(v^T g v).
The set of vectors of unit length under g: an ellipse.
The squared stretch factors along the principal axes; the ellipse's semi-axes are their inverse square roots.
Unequal size in different directions: the ellipse is not a circle.
A small shape used as a mark to encode several numbers at once (size, shape, angle).
A metric tensor that varies smoothly from point to point.

remember: Small ellipse = long cost = large eigenvalue.
Always draw a reference circle for g = I.
State the convention; the inverse tensor gives the opposite picture.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: Each ellipse is a mark with a position, a size, an aspect ratio and an orientation. Together these show the three degrees of freedom of a 2-by-2 symmetric matrix at that point: two eigenvalues and an angle. The dashed reference circle fixes the unit.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: A metric says how long vectors are, which is not constant in a curved or deformed space. The set of unit vectors is a circle for the plain metric and an ellipse for any other, so drawing ellipses turns a matrix field into a field of shapes the eye reads fast. Where the ellipse is small, a small step already counts as unit length: distance is costly there.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: People often read big as 'large metric' when it is the reverse. Overlapping ellipses hide shapes. A grid hides what happens between points. And the scale factor (here 0.21) is arbitrary, so ellipse sizes are meaningful only relative to the reference circle.

understand.title: Why each required item matters
understand.text: The reference circle gives absolute meaning. The scale legend fixes the unit. A note on convention prevents the inverse-reading error. All three are about preventing a sign or inverse mistake.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: To show directions only use eigenvector line segments; for scalar summaries use a heat map of det g (the area factor) or the condition number (F2.3). For a map the corresponding glyph is the Tissot indicatrix: the image of a unit circle. For tensor fields in mechanics use stress or strain ellipses.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Colour each ellipse by its determinant and add short axes lines for the eigenvector directions, with the larger axis of each drawn as a thick segment.

steps.title: Length and the unit ball
steps.note: In the eigenbasis the condition v^T g v = 1 reads lambda1 a^2 + lambda2 b^2 = 1: an ellipse with semi-axes 1/sqrt(lambda1) and 1/sqrt(lambda2).

steps.title: Numbers from the render
steps.note: Semi-axes in units of the reference radius. Moving right and up, the eigenvalues grow, so ellipses shrink; at (4, 0) the ratio 1 to 0.577 is the strongest anisotropy.

worked.title: Reading the reference render
worked.problem: From the figure: (1) where is distance cheapest? (2) Where are the ellipses most elongated? (3) Where is distance almost isotropic but costly?

solution.text: Bottom-left, near (0, 0): the largest ellipses, semi-axes 1 and 0.85 times the reference radius (eigenvalues 1 and 1.4).
Along the bottom right edge at (4, 0), where the eigenvalues are 1 and 3: the ratio of axes is 1 to 0.58, tilted by phi = 0.8 rad.
Top-right, near (4, 3): eigenvalues 3.0 and 3.2, nearly round, with semi-axes about 0.58 and 0.56: costly, about 1.7 times the Euclidean cost, in every direction.

worked.answer: Cheapest at the bottom-left, most anisotropic at the bottom-right, costly and nearly isotropic at the top-right.

checks.q: What does a small ellipse mean in this picture?
checks.answer: A short step already has unit length under the metric: distance is costly in that direction.
